name: Wendy Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Wendy. I'm a researcher at the Work Futures Panel, which is independent: no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could we start with a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run press line three at Corvane Appliances. We stamp the steel panels for washing machines and dryers, the sides and the tops. There are four big presses in a row, the biggest is six hundred tonnes, and the sheet goes through them one after another until it's a panel. I'm team lead on days, so I'm in at quarter to six for the handover, then I'm doing die changes, quality checks, and making sure nobody puts their hand where it shouldn't go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like die changes, honestly. We've got it down to twenty-two minutes on line three, the best in the plant, and I trained everyone who does it. What wears me out is the noise and that every month is the same balancing act. Tom drives for a delivery company, I'm on lower pay than the leads at Corvane's other site, and we've got about two weeks of money in the bank. We've been trying to save a deposit for a flat for three years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I used one to sort out the holiday rota when everyone wanted August. And Tom made me use it to write a complaint to the energy company, which actually worked. I don't use it at work much, there's not much it can do on a press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. Sounds like most new things, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful for a few things and then everyone calmed down. I'd say it at work in the canteen, probably while someone's showing a video of some robot doing a backflip. Online I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, fine by me. It means the plan we've got still works. Keep the job, keep saving, get the flat in two or three years. That's the whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd push again for the lead allowance to match the other site, because that's forty a week we're missing. And I'd keep putting the hundred a month into the flat account, which is slow but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a plan staying on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the lead allowance different at the other site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: History, apparently. They were a different company before Corvane bought them, and nobody ever evened it out. HR keeps saying it's under review. It's been under review since I got promoted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the flat mean to you and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A place where the landlord can't put the rent up whenever he likes. He did it twice last year. And honestly, a place where we can think about kids one day without worrying about being kicked out.

S0.say: AI was useful for a few things and then everyone calmed down. That's what I'd say in the canteen while someone shows a robot doing a backflip.
S0.think: It's fine by me, because our plan still works. Keep the job, keep saving and get the flat in two or three years.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is and pushes HR again for the lead allowance to match the other site, worth 40 a week. Keeps putting 100 a month into the flat deposit account.
S0.feel: Calm, like a plan staying on track.
S0.quote: It's been under review since I got promoted.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's life is organised around one slow plan: a flat deposit with her partner Tom. The hype picture keeps that plan intact, so she's calm. Her grievance is an unexplained pay gap with Corvane's other site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more like what's actually happening. We've got a robot arm on line one already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's make it work. At work I'd say the people who know the presses should be trained on the new kit first. I'm not going to fight it, but I'm not going to pretend it's free either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm more worried about Tom than me. Line one's robot moves the panels between presses, but it still needs someone who knows how to change the dies and spot a split. Delivery, though, the company is already testing those little robot vans in the city. If his work shrinks, we're on my pay alone, and my pay alone doesn't get us a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd go and watch line one properly, see how they set the robot up and what goes wrong. If it works, I'd ask to be trained on it before it comes to line three. I'd want the press maintenance certificate too, if Corvane pays. And Tom and I would try to save a bit faster, maybe a hundred and fifty, in case his hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, more like keeping an eye on the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go and watch line one first. What would convince you it works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they run a full week without calling the robot company out. Right now the engineer from the robot firm is in our canteen more than some of our own staff. When he stops coming, it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Tom said anything about the robot vans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He jokes about it. He says they can't carry a fridge up four flights of stairs. But he did ask me last week how I got my forklift licence, so I think he's thinking about it.

S1.say: It's coming whether we like it or not, so let's make it work. The people who know the presses should be trained first, and it isn't free just because it's new.
S1.think: I'm more worried about Tom's delivery job than mine, because robot vans are already being tested. If his work shrinks, my pay alone won't get us a flat.
S1.do: Watches the robot arm on line one until it runs a week without outside help, then asks to be trained on it and to get the press maintenance certificate if Corvane pays. Raises the couple's savings to about 150 a month in case Tom's hours drop.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping an eye on the sky.
S1.quote: Right now the engineer from the robot firm is in our canteen more than some of our own staff.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy thinks about risk as a household, and her partner's delivery job worries her more than her own. She'll adopt the robot once it has proved itself, with a clear test: a week without the robot firm's engineer. Tom asking about her forklift licence suggests he's quietly worried too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Both of us, then. Him and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be handled properly, by the government and the companies together. Don't just switch people off. I'd say it calmly, because shouting doesn't change anything, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the flat's gone. Not delayed, gone. If his van drives itself and my presses run themselves, we've got two weeks of money and two jobs that don't exist. There's maybe a year of overlap where they still need people like me to babysit the robots, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the flat money, about three thousand six hundred, and make it the emergency fund. I'd stop the gym, the phone contracts would go to the cheapest ones. I'd look at the hospital, because they have a maintenance department and someone has to fix the beds, at least at first. And I'd look into what support there is, without being too proud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. And angry at myself, a bit, for not doing more sooner, even though I know I couldn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said angry at yourself. What would you have done sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. I did everything right. Got the diploma, got promoted, saved every month. That's what makes it so annoying. There was no right thing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right, which I wouldn't know. Then we'd make a list on the back of an envelope, that's how we do money. Every big decision we've made started on the back of an envelope.

S2.say: This has to be handled properly by the government and companies together, without just switching people off. Shouting doesn't change anything, but I'd say it.
S2.think: The flat isn't delayed, it's gone. With two weeks of money and both jobs automated, there's maybe a year where they still need someone to babysit the robots.
S2.do: Turns the 3,600 flat fund into an emergency fund, drops the gym and switches to the cheapest phone plans. Looks for work in the hospital's maintenance department and checks what public support exists.
S2.feel: Sick, and a bit angry at herself even though she knows she did everything right.
S2.quote: Every big decision we've made started on the back of an envelope.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI hits Wendy as a double loss: both her press line and Tom's van go at once. Giving up the flat fund was the moment she sounded most shaken. Her anger at herself for doing everything right shows how much she trusted the steady path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight, but it's a bit of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we know it's coming, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. Companies should be training people now, and I'd say so at work. I'd ask my manager what Corvane's plan is, straight out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to see if things work before I jump, which is how I like to do it. The robots would come to line one first, then the others. I'd have two or three years of watching before line three changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the maintenance certificate in the first year, because fixing machines will last longer than running them. Tom and I would decide together whether we still buy the flat, maybe a smaller one, maybe further out where it's cheap. I'd keep saving the hundred a month and try to push it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's a problem with a shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A smaller flat further out. What would that mean day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A longer drive, maybe forty minutes instead of fifteen. Tom's mum lives out that way, so it's not all bad. But I'd hate to buy something just as the jobs disappear and get stuck with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you buy it or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. That's the honest answer. We'd talk about it for a year, probably, and then decide on the back of an envelope like always.

S3.say: We know it's coming, so there's no excuse for being caught out. I'd ask my manager straight out what Corvane's plan is.
S3.think: Five years is enough to see if things work before I jump, which is how I like it. I'd have two or three years of watching before line three changes.
S3.do: Gets the press maintenance certificate in the first year, betting that fixing machines lasts longer than running them. Rethinks the flat with Tom, perhaps smaller and further out, and tries to raise their 100 a month in savings.
S3.feel: Anxious, but it's a problem with a shape she can work on.
S3.quote: Fixing machines will last longer than running them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Wendy's watch-then-move approach, and she'd use it to get a maintenance certificate. The flat decision becomes genuinely uncertain: she's afraid of taking on a mortgage just as jobs vanish. She was candid that she didn't know whether they'd buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so let's do it properly. People need training, and there should be some kind of support for when the work runs out. I'd say it in a normal voice, not like the world's ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be fine for a good while. I'd buy the flat, actually, in this one. Ten years of payments while I still have work makes a dent, and I'd have time to change jobs maybe twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the maintenance certificate, then probably move into maintenance at Corvane for a few years. Tom and I would buy the flat, small, and pay extra off the mortgage when we can. Around year five I'd look at what's still a human job and train for that, whatever it turns out to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly normal. It's like knowing your car's got five years left in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat with ten years but not sure with five. What tips it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten, I'd pay off a chunk before anything happens. With five, I'd barely have started. The bank doesn't care that the robots are coming, it just wants its money every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Tom, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to move from vans to something else. He's good with people, he always gets the tips at Christmas. Maybe something where talking to people matters. I'd push him to start looking early, he leaves things late.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do it properly, so let's do it properly. People need training and some kind of support for when the work runs out.
S4.think: I'd probably be fine for a good while, and I'd actually buy the flat in this one. Ten years of payments while I still have work makes a dent.
S4.do: Gets the maintenance certificate and moves into maintenance at Corvane for a few years. Buys a small flat with Tom and overpays the mortgage when possible, then around year five trains for whatever is still a human job.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly normal, like knowing the car has five years left.
S4.quote: The bank doesn't care that the robots are coming, it just wants its money every month.
S4.fieldNote: The warning time directly flips Wendy's biggest decision: no flat with two years, unsure with five, buy with ten. She plans in stages and pushes Tom to start early because he leaves things late. Her calm here depends on having time to pay down debt before work runs out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It takes both our jobs at once and the flat with them, and we've only got two weeks of money. What would help is a bridge: something that pays you while you retrain, and some honesty from employers about their plans so you can see it coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. Everyone asks about one person's job. But it's households that sink. If it's just me, I can manage. If it's me and Tom at the same time, the envelope doesn't add up.

headlineQuote: If it's me and Tom at the same time, the envelope doesn't add up.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old press line lead at an appliance factory, proud of the fastest die change in the plant but paid less than leads at the company's other site. She and her partner Tom, a delivery driver, have about two weeks of money in the bank and have been saving for a flat for three years. She adopts new things once they've proved themselves, and she thinks about risk as a household. Fast AGI would wipe out both their jobs and the flat at once, which alarms her. With five or ten years she plans a maintenance certificate, and with a decade she'd go ahead and buy the flat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both her job and Tom's at once, and the flat with them, with only two weeks of money saved.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge that pays people while they retrain, and honesty from employers about their plans so workers can see change coming.
